ask.changes_what: Shaking chills should prompt blood cultures and a search for a bacteremic source (line, biliary, urinary, endovascular); no chills supports withholding cultures when pretest probability is low.
ask.do_not_use_when: The RCE conclusions do not apply to immunocompromised patients or when endocarditis is suspected; in those groups obtain cultures regardless of chills.
ask.escalation_warning: Rigors with hypotension, altered mentation or a central line indicate probable bacteremia/sepsis: cultures, source control and antibiotics within the hour.

evidence.citation: Coburn B, Morris AM, Tomlinson G, Detsky AS. Does this adult patient with suspected bacteremia require blood cultures? JAMA. 2012;308(5):502-511.
evidence.population: Adult immunocompetent patients in whom bacteremia was suspected (35 studies; 4566 bacteremia and 25,946 negative episodes)
evidence.quote: The severity of chills graded on an ordinal scale (shaking chills, LR, 4.7; 95% CI, 3.0-7.2) may be more useful.

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: Shaking chills showed a specificity of 90.3% (95% CI 89.2-91.5) and positive likelihood ratio of 4.65 (95% CI 2.95-6.86).
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: shaking chills (whole-body shaking under a thick blanket)

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: The absence of chills showed a sensitivity of 87.5% (95% CI 74.4-94.5) and negative likelihood ratio of 0.24 (95% CI 0.11-0.51).
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: any chills (sensitivity and LR- refer to absence of chills)

ask.how: Ask the patient (or witnesses) whether they have had chills and grade the worst episode: mild = feeling cold, needing a jacket; moderate = needing a thick blanket; shaking chills = whole-body shaking even under a thick blanket. Record timing relative to fever and any line, procedure or infusion.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of any chills lowers the probability of bacteremia (LR- 0.24) but does not exclude it, particularly in elderly or immunocompromised patients who may not mount rigors.
ask.pitfalls: Rigors also occur with malaria, transfusion or drug reactions, and after amphotericin or contaminated infusions; the grading relies on patient recall and the RCE data exclude immunocompromised patients and suspected endocarditis.
ask.positive_finding: Shaking (rigor-grade) chills raise the probability of bacteremia about 4.7-fold (LR+ 4.7, 95% CI 3.0-7.2; specificity 0.90) and justify blood cultures before antibiotics.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or witness able to describe the episode; ask before antipyretics blunt recall.
ask.rationale: Rigors suggest bacteremia and help prioritize blood cultures and search for a source.
ask.title: Rigors / shaking chills

ask.changes_what: Positive: stop the suspect drug (substitute if needed), expect defervescence within ~72 h, continue infection work-up. Negative: keep searching for occult infection, thrombosis or malignancy.
ask.contraindications: Do not stop essential drugs (e.g., antimicrobials for a proven infection, immunosuppressants) without a risk-benefit assessment.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not attribute fever to a drug in a neutropenic, septic or haemodynamically unstable patient until infection has been excluded; do not withdraw life-sustaining drugs on this basis alone.
ask.escalation_warning: Fever with rash, mucosal involvement, facial oedema, eosinophilia or organ dysfunction may be DRESS/SJS: stop the drug immediately and escalate.
ask.how: Build a dated medication timeline (start/stop of every agent, including antibiotics, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, heparin) against the fever curve. Look for fever beginning after a new drug, a patient who looks relatively well despite high temperatures, a pulse lower than expected for the temperature, rash or eosinophilia, and defervescence within about 72 h of stopping the suspect drug.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of rash, eosinophilia or relative bradycardia does not argue against drug fever: these accompaniments were found in only a minority of cases in the largest series. Persistence of fever more than a few days after stopping the suspect drug argues against the diagnosis.
ask.pitfalls: Textbook features (relative bradycardia, rash, eosinophilia, characteristic fever pattern) are absent in most cases; drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion and infection must be ruled out first. Rechallenge reproduces fever and is usually inappropriate.
ask.positive_finding: Fever temporally following a new drug, with no alternative source and resolution after withdrawal, supports drug fever; antibacterials (beta-lactams, vancomycin, rifampicin, aminoglycosides) are the commonest culprits and median onset is about 2 days but the lag is highly variable.
ask.prerequisites: Complete medication reconciliation; other infectious and non-infectious causes actively sought and excluded.
ask.rationale: A temporal link between fever and new drugs can point toward drug fever, which may change management.
ask.title: Fever onset temporally linked to a new drug (with rash/relative bradycardia)

examine.changes_what: A positive survey targets cultures, imaging and source control (line removal, drainage, debridement); a negative survey mandates blood/urine cultures and imaging rather than reassurance.
examine.contraindications: None; do not delay cultures and antibiotics in suspected sepsis while completing the survey.
examine.do_not_use_when: Never let a negative source survey withhold cultures, empiric antibiotics or imaging in a hypotensive, febrile or acutely confused patient with suspected infection.
examine.escalation_warning: Crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis or pain out of proportion (necrotizing fasciitis), a hot joint, peritonism, or purulence at a central line/dialysis catheter in a septic patient require immediate surgical/source-control and line removal decisions.
examine.how: Undress and inspect every line, dialysis and drain/exit site (erythema, purulence, tunnel tenderness), all skin including back, sacrum, heels, perineum, injection sites and wounds; palpate abdomen (peritonism, Murphy sign, flank tenderness), joints and spine for warmth/effusion/tenderness; check urinary catheter, mouth, sinuses, ears and chest. Repeat daily while the source is unknown.
examine.negative_finding: A normal survey does not exclude an occult source: insertion-site inflammation is absent in nearly all catheter-related bloodstream infections, and intra-abdominal, urinary, endovascular and spinal infections are frequently silent in elderly, immunosuppressed or sedated patients.
examine.pitfalls: Line-site appearance has near-zero sensitivity for CRBSI (coagulase-negative staphylococci cause little inflammation); steroids, neutropenia and neuropathy blunt local signs; dressings, obesity and immobility hide sacral, perineal and injection-site infections. Pain out of proportion with unimpressive skin findings suggests necrotizing infection.
examine.positive_finding: Purulence, spreading erythema or tunnel tenderness at a line/exit site, cellulitis or crepitus, a hot swollen joint, peritonism or flank tenderness, or a sacral/heel ulcer with surrounding infection identifies a probable source and directs cultures, source control and empiric therapy.
examine.prerequisites: Full exposure with dressings taken down, adequate lighting and analgesia; review lines, catheters and devices with their insertion dates; log-roll immobile patients to view the sacrum.
examine.rationale: A focused source exam can rapidly identify or rule out obvious infection sources (catheter, wound, lungs, skin).
examine.title: Focused infection-source exam (line/exit sites, skin, abdomen, joints, sacrum, urine catheter)

examine.changes_what: Focal egophony in a febrile, coughing patient raises pneumonia probability substantially (LR+ about 6); proceed to CXR/LUS and empiric treatment as clinically indicated.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of egophony to withhold imaging in a patient with hypoxia, abnormal vital signs or immunocompromise.
examine.escalation_warning: Egophony plus hypotension, RR >30 or confusion suggests severe pneumonia; assess for sepsis and consider admission.

evidence.citation: Ebell MH, Chupp H, Cai X, Bentivegna M, Kearney M. Accuracy of signs and symptoms for the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia: a meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2020;27(7):541-553.
evidence.population: Adults with clinically suspected pneumonia or acute cough; 17 prospective cohorts (9 primary care, 7 ED); CAP prevalence 10% primary care, 20% ED

examine.how: Auscultate the posterior and lateral chest while the patient repeatedly says a sustained 'ee'; egophony is present where the sound is heard as a nasal 'ay' (A) over a focal area but as 'ee' elsewhere. Compare with breath sounds at the same site for a harsh, tubular bronchial quality with a pause between inspiration and expiration.
examine.negative_finding: Normal vesicular sounds and 'ee' transmitted unchanged; absence has little rule-out value because the sign is insensitive.
examine.pitfalls: Sensitivity is low so most pneumonias lack egophony; it also occurs over the compressed lung at the upper border of a pleural effusion and can be mimicked at the trachea and interscapular area in thin patients.
examine.positive_finding: Focal E-to-A change and/or bronchial breath sounds over lung parenchyma, indicating consolidation or the compressed lung above an effusion.
examine.prerequisites: Cooperative patient able to phonate; compare with the contralateral side at the same level.
examine.rationale: Egophony helps detect focal consolidation, supporting or refuting pneumonia as a source of fever.
examine.title: Egophony (E-to-A change) or bronchial breath sounds over a focal area

examine.changes_what: Unilateral warm erythema: treat as cellulitis but rule out DVT/necrotizing infection; bilateral: seek pseudocellulitis (stasis, dermatitis) before antibiotics.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use asymmetry/border to reassure when there is severe pain, rapid progression, bullae, crepitus, hypotension or immunocompromise; necrotizing infection needs surgical evaluation regardless of score.
examine.escalation_warning: Unilateral swollen warm leg also fits DVT: obtain compression ultrasound if no clear portal of entry or if edema dominates over erythema.

evidence.citation: Pulia MS, Schwei RJ, Alexandridis R, et al. Validation of Thermal Imaging and the ALT-70 Prediction Model to Differentiate Cellulitis From Pseudocellulitis. JAMA Dermatol. 2024;160(5):511-517.
evidence.population: Adults presenting to ED with acute lower-extremity dermatologic symptoms, n=204, 92 with cellulitis
evidence.reference_standard: Independent 6-physician consensus review of the case
evidence.target_condition: Lower-extremity cellulitis vs pseudocellulitis (ALT-70 model; asymmetry item weighted 3 points)

evidence.citation: Raff AB, Weng QY, Cohen JM, et al. A predictive model for diagnosis of lower extremity cellulitis: A cross-sectional study. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2017;76(4):618-625.e2.
evidence.population: Patients admitted via ED with a diagnosis of lower-extremity cellulitis, n=259, 2010-2012
evidence.quote: In total, 79 (30.5%) of 259 patients were misdiagnosed with lower extremity cellulitis
evidence.reference_standard: Discharge diagnosis (cellulitis vs alternative diagnosis) after inpatient evaluation

examine.how: Expose and compare both legs. Note whether erythema is unilateral (asymmetric) or bilateral, feel for warmth with the back of the hand against the contralateral limb, and trace the border (marking it with pen for follow-up). Check for a portal of entry (tinea, ulcer), tenderness, and disproportionate pain, crepitus or bullae.
examine.negative_finding: Bilateral symmetric erythema without fever, leukocytosis or tachycardia favors stasis dermatitis or other pseudocellulitis (ALT-70 0-2 points: >=83% pseudocellulitis); bilateral cellulitis is rare.
examine.pitfalls: ALT-70 is sensitive but only 22% specific in a prospective ED validation, so a 'positive' asymmetric leg still includes many DVT, gout, contact dermatitis and stasis cases; warmth is subjective; do not miss necrotizing infection (pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus).
examine.positive_finding: Unilateral warm, tender erythema, especially with leukocytosis, tachycardia or age >=70 (ALT-70 >=5 points), gives >=82% likelihood of true cellulitis in the derivation cohort. Asymmetry is the heaviest-weighted item (3 points).
examine.prerequisites: Both legs exposed; heart rate, temperature and WBC available if scoring ALT-70.
examine.rationale: Checking for unilateral erythema helps identify cellulitis, especially post-op or near surgical sites.
examine.title: Unilateral warm erythema with defined border (vs bilateral / stasis change)

examine.changes_what: A hot swollen joint with painful passive motion should trigger urgent aspiration (cell count, crystals, Gram stain, culture) and orthopedic review; do not treat as cellulitis.
examine.contraindications: Do not force range of motion in a suspected fracture or unstable prosthesis.
examine.do_not_use_when: Never use absence of fever or a modest exam to exclude septic arthritis; prosthetic joints and immunosuppressed patients need aspiration on suspicion alone.
examine.escalation_warning: Hot swollen joint with fever, rigors, sepsis physiology, IV drug use or a prosthesis requires same-day aspiration and orthopedic/ID involvement; delayed treatment destroys the joint.

evidence.citation: Margaretten ME, Kohlwes J, Moore D, Bent S. Does this adult patient have septic arthritis? JAMA. 2007;297(13):1478-1488.
evidence.population: Adults presenting with an acutely painful and/or swollen joint (14 studies, 6242 patients, 653 with septic arthritis)
evidence.quote: Joint pain (sensitivity, 85%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 78%-90%), a history of joint swelling (sensitivity, 78%; 95% CI, 71%-85%)
evidence.reference_standard: Gold standard for septic arthritis (positive synovial fluid or blood culture / clinical criteria as defined by included studies)
evidence.target_condition: Nongonococcal bacterial (septic) arthritis - finding: joint pain

evidence.citation: Margaretten ME, Kohlwes J, Moore D, Bent S. Does this adult patient have septic arthritis? JAMA. 2007;297(13):1478-1488.
evidence.population: Adults presenting with an acutely painful and/or swollen joint (14 studies, 6242 patients, 653 with septic arthritis)
evidence.quote: fever (sensitivity, 57%; 95% CI, 52%-62%) are the only findings that occur in more than 50% of patients
evidence.reference_standard: Gold standard for septic arthritis (positive synovial fluid or blood culture / clinical criteria as defined by included studies)

examine.how: Expose and compare both joints: inspect for swelling and erythema, palpate for warmth and an effusion (patellar tap or bulge sign at the knee, fullness at other joints), then move the joint passively through its range. Note pain with small passive movements, restriction, and whether the patient will bear weight on the limb.
examine.negative_finding: No exam finding rules out septic arthritis; fever is absent in over 40% of cases, and specificity of these findings against gout, pseudogout or reactive arthritis is low.
examine.pitfalls: Cellulitis over a joint, crystal arthritis and hemarthrosis look identical; pain on passive motion favors joint involvement over cellulitis. Elderly, immunosuppressed and prosthetic-joint patients may have muted findings.
examine.positive_finding: An acutely painful, swollen, warm joint with effusion and painful limited passive motion is the expected picture of septic arthritis (joint pain sensitivity 0.85, joint swelling 0.78, fever 0.57) and mandates arthrocentesis before antibiotics.
examine.prerequisites: Adequate exposure of both sides; assess before analgesia blunts findings when feasible.
examine.rationale: Examining for a hot, swollen joint is crucial post-arthroplasty to rule out septic arthritis.
examine.title: Hot swollen joint with effusion and painful/limited range of motion (refusal to bear weight)
